Mr. Chairman, when we were dealing with this item last night I was pointing out that the war expenditures committee had brought in a report stating that it was the intention to call the committee together again at the next session. We think it advisable that this or some other committee continue the investigation of War Assets Corporation between now and the time any such committee may be set up at the next session. The sales and operations of the War Assets Corporation leave a great deal to be desired so far as public information is concerned. Purchasers throughout Canada who try to obtain materials from War Assets Corporation find that there is very little information as to what supplies are available. Something of a run-around is being given to these people.
We were told in the committee that a certain price structure had been set up and that a certain policy was being followed in connection with the pricing of commodities, but those who have endeavoured to buy articles from this corporation find that that is not the policy that is followed. People may be asked to make a bid for certain articles but when they try to get hold of them they are told that someone else has purchased them. It is evident that someone has a priority, that someone higher up has the power to sell these commodities and they are withdrawn from the market overnight.

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The policy of merchandising wras dealt with fully in the committee.

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I agree that is so, but the policy outlined in the committee is not the policy that is followed with these people who are trying to purchase material. As I say, there is a difference between the actual operations of the corporation and the policy that was supposed to be laid down. Take machine tools, for instance. ' When people tried to purchase these they found that they were not available, or that they were available only to dealers or agents. There appears to be a division of authority. These people find either that War Assets Corporation has no power to sell this material, or that someone higher up has already made a deal. On September 24 I placed a question on the order paper asking:

Supply-Reconstruction
What was the total value of the buildings, equipment, supplies, and other materials:	(a)
sold; (b) exchanged; (c) loaned; (d) leased; (e) otherwise disposed *of by the Minister of Munitions and Supply as of August 31, 1945, under the -Surplus Crown Assets Act?
What is the total amount received by the government for the materials referred to in question 1 ?
That question, was never answered by the committee, and the committee is to be disbanded with the prorogation of parliament. Apparently that information is not to be given. There is a question on the order paper at the present time which I placed there on November 12 and which has not been answered at this late day. It reads;
What persons or companies, if any. have been paid or allowed commission by War Assets Corporation on sales or exchange of goods by that corporation?
What is the amount of commission to each person or company?
Apparently that question is not to be answered. The War Assets Corporation published an annual report as from July 12, 1944 to March 31, 1945. Apparently this corporation has changed completely in its personnel. There seems to be practically an entire new company in operation, because we find this on page 5 of the report:
To obtain the complete picture of surplus disposals in Canada there should be added to the record of the corporation the surplus disposal operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply prior to the formation of the corporation and later running in parallel with it, and there should also be added transactions negotiated by the director general of war surpluses, Department of Reconstruction, Ottawa.
These three operations added together show a total volume of material disposed of amounting to $19,768,000 divided as follows:
As to what that material was and what the original cost of it was, we are given no information. We do not know what kind of deals were made; we do not know what the material was originally worth. On page 12 we find an analysis of sales. In the case of real estate all the information given is that there were two sales of a total amount of $13,000. What good is that? We want to find out whether the Canadian people are getting proper value from these sales. It says there were 2,086 sales of scrap metal totalling $1,257,568.15. For trucks and tractors, there were 1,107 sales-this could mean 11,000 trucks-totalling $871,366.63. There were 1,555 sales of ferrous metals, totalling $840,180.08. That sort of information is not good enough. As I said, the people of Canada were ready to spend money lavishly to win the war. The war had to be won and war is a costly business. Apparently there is a lot of
monkey business in it as well. The Canadian people will deeply resent the giving away oi the handing over of assets valued at billions of dollars without a proper accounting. The kind of thing that makes us suspicious is what is set out in a press report from Washington which appeared in yesterday's papers. This reads:
Britons, Canadians who were in Britain, and perhaps some Americans will be a little dismayed to learn that the gasoline used by the Luftwaffe bombers which droned over London every night early in the war was "made in U.S.A." So were the casings_ of thousands of the magnesium fire bombs which were used in the fire blitzes.
A war department report presented to a special -Senate committee here says that I.G. Farben, vast German chemical trust, exploited cartel agreements with American companies to make nazi armies self-sufficient in^ strategic materials needed to start and maintain the war. From the United States it^ got new methods for making components of high octane gasoline including tetraethyl lead, and when it could not make tetraethyl lead in time for the start of the war in 1939, it got 500 tons from the Ethyl Export Corporation of the United States.
The report goes on to say that the I.G. Farben company found ways to make through chemistry what was not readily available in Germany. It goes on:
Other things, which it could not make, I.G, Farben obtained through its cartel cohorts in foreign countries.
One of the greatest of these was Standard Oil of New Jersey, which made known to I.G. Farben its revolutionary process of producing iso-octane and utilizing it for motor fuels.
One of the German scientists said in a report brought to light by the War Department investigating committee "production of iso-ootane originated entirely with the Americans and became known to us in detail in its separate stages through our agreement with Standard Oil Company of New Jersey and is being used extensively by us. The process for producing tetraethyl lead, essential for the manufacture of aviation gasoline was obtained in exactly the same way."	_ _
In addition -to making and stockpiling magnesium for bomb castings, the report says Farben Company purchased large stocks of magnesium from the Dow Chemical Corporation of America to build up its reserves for the Luftwaffe.
Farben had about 2,0-00 cartel arrangements including some with Aluminum Company of America, E. I. Dupont de Nemours. Imperial Chemical Industries of Great Britain, and companies in France and Japan.
It is evident that in the operation of a war there are people who make money out of it, and it is beginning to dawn on the peoples of the world that until we take the profits out of war it will be difficult to end war. When this war is over I think the people of Canada are going to demand a complete investigation of War Assets Corporation to find out what is happening to our assets, who is obtaining
Supply-Reconstruction

them, and whether Canada is making a good bargain in their disposal. So far as this house is concerned we have no information on these things. It is very difficult to get information. That is why I ask the minister to see that a committee of this house, or perhaps the very committee that was set up to investigate War Assets Corporation, be allowed, under the powers granted to the government by the special powers bill, to continue its investigation.
I personally wanted to visit some of the War Assets plants. I was informed by the minister that he could not give me a blanket pass to visit the plants but that War Assets would have to be notified in advance. He was willing to give me an introduction to the manager of any plant operated by War Assets if I would notify them when I was coming, and would make arrangements for me to make a tour of the plants.
What we need is a committee with power to go around and visit War Assets plants. We do not want this investigation shut off for another three months. That only means that when we come back here the barn door will be open and the horse gone. I would ask the minister to make a statement.

I want to say a word or two about the committee that was_ appointed to investigate War Assets Corporation, and the reason I want to do it is that I feel that I have been called upon as a member of that committee to take part in a solemn farce. I wonder if parliament wants to leave that situation as it is. What do I mean by a solemn farce? I will try to state it briefly.
This committee was set up with twenty-five members, a very sensible lot of men; they looked to me quite sensible. We sat in a large room and I felt quite important, almost as if I were at a peace conference. The newspaper men were all there, solemnly taking down what we said. Official reporters were there taking down our every word as if the whole thing was important. Senior civil servants were there, running in and out. You really felt that something was stirring. I was so much impressed that I believe I wrote a letter to the chairman saying that I felt pleased that something was really going to be done. If I did, hon. gentlemen will be amused about that, though as I look back I do not know whether to be amused or indignant.-either one or the other; one either should laugh or be angry. Why? What happened? We had eight meetings. Several of the meetings toward the end were held while the house was sitting, and unless you can split yourself in two or three pieces, and I could not do that, vertically anyway, you

could attend only one thing at.a time, the house or the committee. In the committee we were given statements by officials of War Assets Corporation, a sensible lot of statements; I had no quarrel with what they said. I think those officials were good men, and what they were doing seemed sensible. But it was made clear that they were not actually dealing with the important things; these were dealt with by the Minister of Reconstruction. I do not know how he deals with them when he is in Bermuda attending an air conference, and if I may digress for a moment I want to say what I said in the house once before that unless the Minister of Reconstruction can split himself in four he cannot do efficiently what he is attempting to do to-day.

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: He is doing a mighty good job.

The minister will speak to that. W'hat I am talking about now is what the committee has done, or rather did not do. The committee got these statements, which I thought were very sensible statements. Then I thought we vvere getting to the stage where we. should oe able to get our teeth into, something, or, is one membqr of the committee said, see the work in action. What do I mean? I mean by taking some actual cases.
We had a steering committee, which I thought was going to bring forward some actual cases. We were asked to send cases to the steering committee, and I sent in one or two. What do I mean by cases? Not suggestions of any impropriety. I just mean cases where on the face of it, it looked as if the disposition of a certain property had not been provident, perhaps had been done hurriedly, perhaps with not as great efficiency as might have been.
Let me say again that there was no suggestion of scandal or anything of the kind. It was just a question of trying tb get the committee at work on something. I hope that I shall never be asked to sit on such a committee again. I was told by an experienced parliamentarian when this committee was first set up, "Don't imagine it will ever do anything". But I was young in experience here, and I thought perhaps this was a committee that would be different. I just want to say that it was no different. Up to the present we have not been allowed to do anything of any value because we have just had these general principles, and as the hon. member for York-ton has just said, we were not allowed to see the thing in action.
The way we suggest of seeing it in action is that we should be allowed to go on with

Supply-Reconstruction
our investigation during the recess. I do not know that I agree with the hon. member for Yorkton that we should go around and visit the different plants. I doubt very much that I would be in favour of that. But I would be in favour of having some continuous connected time for our investigation so that we can really deal with this thing. I ask members present whether it was sensible towards the end of the session to appoint a group of men who could meet only eight times many of whom were not able to be there all the time, and who could only hear a story told them, very pleasantly, of certain things that were happening. But the main things never came before that committee because the main things are the sale of plants, going concerns, and that is dealt with by the Minister of Reconstruction. I am not complaining about that. That may be quite all right. But what I am saying is that either the committee should never have been set up at all or it should have been allowed to do something.
I do not want this house to make a fool of itself in the eyes of the public. That is what we are doing. I think that the operation of the committee is inconsistent with the picture that was drawn by the Prime Minister-I wish he were present to hear what I am saying-and with what he said and said so well the other day about the part which this house should play.
I finish as I began, by saying that I object to the history of this committee; I object to our being now dissolved after three or four weeks, for two reasons. First of all, we were just beginning to get 'hot, as the phrase goes, to get to a position where we could have gone ahead with some intelligence. Now we are going away for two or three months, and when we come back I suppose it will not be possible to set up the committee the first day we return, and if we do, we have a dozen other things to occupy us. This committee is dealing with hundreds of millions of dollars of the assets of the people of this country. One can only look on all this as a bad joke, or something to get angry about, and I alternate between one and the other.

In the civil estimates we have item No. 308, "departmental administration, including expenses incidental to organization, $1,500,000." That was gone into fully at that time. And I cannot see why it should be gone into now. However, as I said a moment ago, some statements were made here this morning which I think should be replied to. The discussion which took place in the committee had to do with the alternatives which were mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Yorkton and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. I do not know whether the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario made a motion, but I do know that the two alternatives suggested to the committee were, first, that they sit after prorogation, and, second, that a royal commission be set up. It was pointed out that if sittings were to take place after prorogation they would be irregular because of the rules and proceedings of this house. As for a royal commission, I cannot see how a royal commission would be of any value at this time. Nobody has suggested that there were any scandals, nobody has made any charges, and if there were any charges to make, it was before the committee that they should have been made. The hon. member for Yorkton said in his statement a moment ago, "There is monkey business going on." Well, if there is monkey business going on I think it is up to him to say where the monkey business is, and if on his responsibility as a member of parliament he has any charge to make, let him make it.

I am not asserting that I am. I am merely telling the committee that it is impossible to get from the War Assets Corporation any information concerning the assets which it has for sale. The national income of the whole country before the war was four billions, and we are informed that the assets to be disposed of by this company amount to nearly twenty-five per cent of that huge total. For over a year I for one have been attempting to get information concerning the sale and liquidation of these assets, and whenever I have endeavoured to get information concerning the sale of vehicles, trucks, jeeps and sundiy machinery, invariably there has come a long letter of explanation intimating that this was not the time, this was not the place, perhaps if I wrote to Calgary or to Vancouver, or perhaps if I waited until next fall, or perhaps if I did not bother with it any more I would get as far as I had got. The complaint is that the War Assets Corporation is absolutely beyond the reach of the Canadian people, absolutely beyond the reach of the ordinary member, at least of members of the opposition; and any information that one seeks from the ordinary vendor of materials, any information that one seeks from any large distributor of materials on this continent, is not forthcoming. It is that type of conduct, it is that type of arrogance, it is that unwillingness to divulge information to would-be purchasers, that constitutes the basis and the genesis of my complaint.
I point out to the minister that in fairness to the Canadian people, in fairness to his own government, these arbitrary methods should be abolished. It should not be necessary that one be forced to resort to extraordinary methods to get elementary information concerning the purchase of commodities which we are told are offered on an

equal basis to all Canadians. It is that attitude that is resented, that attitude of the War Assets Corporation that is resented by the Canadian people. It is that attitude that makes one wonder, without knowing, if there is something wrong. It is that attitude that makes people say, "Are we living in a democratic country?" Why was this War Assets Corporation set up? It is away beyond the reach of parliament. We are told it is beyond the administrative powers of the minister. It seems to have been set up as a kind of buffer state between parliament and the people. It is because of this attitude that there is a great deal of unrest and uncertainty and a longing that a few rays of sunlight and fresh air be allowed to permeate the transactions of this body.

We got the job done, and the war is over. We thank the government for having piloted us through. Now the people of Canada are demanding certain reconstruction rights which were promised in the years which have passed. We want individual reconstruction pf the veterans, the war workers and the small business man, so as to enable rehabilitation and reconstruction of home and business.
Yet we have this farce-and I like that word, as used by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, because it is only too true-of talking about houses when people do not have a place to rest. As a new member I am amazed when I listen to the solemn talk which takes place in connection with these matters, when the job of government should be to get -to grips with actual realities. The Liberals have said that they are business people and that they will see the job through and reconstruct Canada. I say that in no small measure we have here the means of reconstruction. Through War Assets Corporation many individuals and small businesses which suffered most as a result of the war could receive a great measure of reconstruction.
During the session dozens of questions were asked of the Minister of Reconstruction as to what was happening with these huge surpluses of commodities. Each one of them was solemnly evaded with the promise that an opportunity would be given to the war expenditures committee, when set up, to investigate every matter fully. And so very late in this session, the government saw fit to establish that committee, of which I was a member. It held its first meeting on November 13, and adjourned a week. It met for one hour and fifteen minutes twice a week for eight complete weeks, and then at its last meeting sat in camera, to prepare the report which was presented to the house.-and1 which, in essence, said nothing more than that we had met, and that we hoped some day to meet again.

May I at this time rush through some criticisms-and I hesitate to go quickly, because this matter is too important to discuss hurriedly. These are my observations as to what happened in committee, or what failed
to happen. The word "farce" still applies, and I thank the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario for it.
From questions asked in committee I am satisfied that there has been considerable disposal of war assets by the Minister of Reconstruction without prior knowledge or recommendation of the officials of War Assets Corporation.
Second, the staff is not familiar with the duties of other departments of War Assets Corporation. That is, there seems to be no interdepartmental liaison.
Third, the reconstruction needs of special areas or groups have not been considered. Perhaps I may be permitted to give one example, namely farm tractors. The list of vehicles sold by the automotive branch, as explained to us on November 27, indicated that 189 farm tractors had been disposed of by War Assets Corporation; 40 of which were sold in Quebec, 102 in Ontario, one in New Brunswick, two in Nova Scotia, two in Prince Edward Island, 28 in Manitoba, one in Saskatchewan, 12 in Alberta, and one in British Columbia. That is contrary to the original terms of the policy set out by the Minister of Reconstruction.

the special needs of veterans setting up in business for the first time. In fact, these veterans are definitely discriminated against, because the position taken by the corporation is that only dealers who were in business m 1941 are permitted to buy through the regular channels.
Contrary to the policy expressed by War Assets Corporation, the speculator is not being kept out of the picture. This applies particularly to machine tools which are being advertised for sale in the leading papers of Montreal and Toronto by people who have bought them from War Assets Corporation. No attention has been paid to the request of departments of education throughout the country for such things as lens equipment, moving picture projectors, radio transmitring equipment, aircraft frames and engines, kitchen equipment, shop tools for manual training, and things of the kind.
I want to be constructive as well as critical. I brought up some of these points in the committee, and I should like now to indicate briefly what this particular branch of government should be doing. I contend that there should be no direct sales made by the Minister of Reconstruction or his staff without prior advertising in the press of Canada. There should be no distribution on a partial geographic basis. There should be no destruction, that is, making scrap out of what to the casual examiner appears to be worth-while equipment, until provincial and municipal bodies and schools have been given a reasonable opportunity to remove this equipment. The one exception to this would be munitions. If priorities are to be continued as a matter of policy, then they should be made effective. When the crown assets allocation committee notifies War Assets that certain materials are to be allotted to it, at the same time notification should be given to the provincial and federal governments. That would mean only ten copies of a slip indicating the material available, its location, whether used or new 'and its approximate value. Those bodies should be given two or three weeks to take up their priority. If it is not taken up, then the material could be made available to the general public, with proper advertising of the full particulars of these surpluses.
To let surplus automobiles be distributed by the automobile manufacturers association of this country is ridiculous. Trucks and other merchandise that might be suitable for veterans should be disposed of through the Department of Veterans Affairs. The Minister of Veterans Affairs assured me the other night that he was taking up actively witl} the Minister of Re-
construction the matter of securing some portion of the tools that are available and which might be used by the veterans. I wish him every success in that. If he does not have any better success in getting that material than we had in getting concrete answers to our questions in the eight meetings of one hour and fifteen minutes each that were held, then the veterans of this country will not receive the consideration that is their due.
A word as to distribution. The ordnance services are still in existence in every military district, and they could be used as distribution agencies for surplus war assets to get these items into the hands of the individuals who need them rather than having them go through the cartels who are going to get them.

If my hon. friend has that conviction, he probably reflects the fact that the Minister of Reconstruction has it in his mind and that the cabinet ministers and some members of the government .have it in theirs; but let me assure him that it is not in the minds of the Canadian people. They want to know just how this colossal disposal of public property is being taken care of. They want to know whether things are being run correctly. As I listened to the hon. member for Verdun and the hon. member for Labelle I thought that they both spoke too long and said too much for their argument. They explained how the war expenditures committee had met to investigate various matters of war expenditures and economies that needed investigating. I understand that committee held eight meetings. Members had given to them for discussion and consideration eight voluminous briefs, each of which would take a long time to analyse. The members of the committee were told that they were privileged to ask questions on the briefs submitted to them.
The committee got certain advice on certain aspects of this situation, and it made a report. No concurrence in that report was moved in this house, and the same is true of the report of any war expenditures committe which has sat since the beginning of the war. There has been no discussion of those reports in detail. That is not enough where we have a government in power for five or six years, a govern-

Supply-Reconstruction
ment which has brought a war to a successful conclusion but which has on hand large volumes of war assets to be disposed of. These are things which are short at the present time; the people are anxious to secure them, and in fairness to everyone I think the greatst publicity should have been given to their disposal.
The government may be sure that everything is all right, and everything may be all right, but I think it would be worth their while having the test of publicity and of public opinion placed upon their actions. If they are so sure that they have the most perfect way of disposing of war assets, they should be ready to convince the members of this parliament that their judgment was right, and through the members of this parliament convince the people of Canada that war assets are being properly, efficiently, wisely and fairly disposed of. That is all we ask; surely that is not asking too much. Even at this late date in the session, if there is anything we can do to get the government to bring publicity to bear on the actions of War Assets Corporation, we will do it. The war expenditures committee has sat for about five years, almost every session since it was first set up.

No one of average intelligence can doubt that we should try to save as much time as we can to-day. If there are no other reasons for it, there is the eagle glare of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Nevertheless what we are doing now is not simply disposing of a few millions or tens of millions of dollars. What we are really doing is considering the whole basis of the expenditure of sums which to me still look astronomical, and I think it is fair to spend a few minutes on that. I regret very much that we are dealing with this matter in the expiring hours of the session, but that is something that we cannot remedy now.
When I spoke on October 19, commenting on the minister's budget speech, I pointed out that to my great surprise there was no statement of affairs, one might call it, given to the Canadian people. We were told the deficit of this year, and if I remember aright we were told the estimated deficit from November of this year to November of next year, but as I said then, we were given a mass of figures really related to nothing. I felt that we should have some estimate from the minister of our national income and some projection into the future. We were not going to hold him to a million or ten million, nevertheless I felt

that we had the right to ask for some statement of our position, and I do hope that we are going to get it now, because I think it is important.
That statement should contain in my opinion a few simple things. It should tell us roughly what we may anticipate in the way of a reduction in the deficit next year, the year after, and so on. I observed with interest that in the budget speech in London of the Chancellor of the Exchequer he grappled in a general way, though only in a general way, with that question, but he did attempt to forecast when they might expect to get to the stage of balancing budgets. Incidentally let me say here-and I think in this the minister will agree with me, if in nothing else that I say-that we hear bandied about now such phrases as "deficit financing", "expanding economy" and so on. These words properly have a place in our financial jargon, our financial vocabulary and perhaps in our financial thinking, but they seem to lead sdme people who ought to know much better to talk as if you could go on borrowing and borrowing without limit. I hear men who ought to know much better comforting themselves by saying, "It is all right so long as we borrow from ourselves." My understanding is that the minister does not agree with that view, and I think it would be well if he would take occasion to say something on it to-day.
I mention these things because it seems to me they go to the very root of the matter. The minister must be perturbed, as every thoughtful man is perturbed, when he considers the astounding heights to which our expenditures have risen. I do not think I need say any more about that now. I shall wait in the hope that the minister may be able to do what I am asking him to do.
As to my second point, I speak as a new member, and perhaps in some ignorance, and part of what I say may appear somewhat naive; if so, I am sorry. I watch these estimates going through and I see hundreds of thousands of dollars being voted for various items-I am referring now in particular to the supplementary estimates, because I assume that they would have had particularly careful scrutiny-and I ask the minister, because I regard the matter as of great importance, to what extent is the Department of Finance really effectively acting as the watchdog of the treasury?
Let me illustrate what I mean. The other night there was an estimate before the committee for some hundreds of thousands of dollars; it came before the committee arid

Supply-Finance
actually there was no explanation given on it until it was asked for from this side. Then an explanation was made in general terms, and it did not seem worth while holding up the business of the committee to crossexamine the minister on this o<r that item.; I do not think we could have done it very intelligently at that point. But can the minister say something to indicate how that sort of thing is handled in his department? When some expenditure is proposed, is it merely a case of the department head saying, "Well, this is a useful expenditure, it will be for the good of the people of Canada"; or is there some yardstick which is being used? Has the minister some budget which he is working to; does he know what we can afford or not afford? Those are two things on which I earnestly hope the minister is able to say something to the committee.

There is another thing I might mention as I am on my feet, although it is really a separate matter. I want the minister to tell us something about the operations of the wartime prices and trade board. I mentioned this to him before. What I suggest is that he might take one of the branches of the department, say food, and let us know how it operates. Also, because I think it is closely related, I should like the minister to say something about the subsidies, and I mean subsidies of all kinds; for example, payments to millers, presumably to keep down the price of flour; payments of freight to bring western grain to the east; all kinds of things which, in my opinion, are in effect subsidies. ^ In elucidating that subject I hope the minister will say whatever he can say as to the policy with regard to subsidies: whether they are confined to the necessaries of life, or as the case may be.
I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs will think I have been commendably brief. I hope the minister will not be so brief, because I v do feel that, in particular, the first question I asked him goes to the very root of the matter. The people of Canada look to him; they respect him; and I would not willingly say anything to add to his burdens. But I think it is one's plain duty to say that we must not be allowed just to wander along hoping for the best. In war time, of course, we had to do that; we could not do anything else. It was not a case of saving money;
indeed it was almost a case of determining how fast could we spend money, because we were spending in order to get the munitions of war. Nobody blamed the minister for *that; everybody praised him for it. But now the shoe is on the other foot. I sympathize with his difficulties, but sometimes I ask myself, with all proper deference, whether it is possible, having spent tens and hundreds of millions of dollars without really looking at both sides of the nickel, to get down to the present task, which is, as I understand it, tc have a plan to work to, and to work to it.

speechtext:
The questions are very fail questions. The trouble is that to answer them at all fully would take a long time, and while I do not object to taking a long time I do not think it is the wish of the committee that I should do so.
With regard to the first question-what are our plans for future budgeting?-the answer cannot be very satisfactory, because we are functioning in an atmosphere of great uncertainty at the present time, owing to the unfinished state1 of the negotiations with the provinces. We made certain offers to the provinces which would involve the assumption of greatly increased social service responsibilities by the dominion government and largely increased1 subsidy payments to the provinces by the dominion government, and we have no idea whether those proposals will be accepted or not. The provinces have made it fairly clear that they will expect our expenditures and subsidies to be much greater than those which we have proposed, and therefore it is impossible for me to be at all definite as to what our uncontrollable expenditures will be over the next few years. I may mention however that during the last year or thereabouts an interdepartmental committee has been sitting considering dominion-provincial relations and payments from the dominion to the provinces and what responsibilities each should assume. Draft budgets-I think I can call them budgets, although they are not detailed at all-have been prepared covering periods two, three or four years hence, and these are based upon various alternative assumptions in respect of national income. That is, they have been based upon the assumption that our'greatest production would be twelve billions or ten billions or eight billions. Perhaps there is another alternative still, but the general principle that will apply to budgeting for the next few years is this, in periods of depressed national income-and by that I do not admit for a moment that we must necessarily have a depression income in any year. But the income in some years will
Supply-Finance

be less than in others. I might describe the years which we shall have to keep in mind as fair, good and excellent, and in a period of high national income we certainly intend to balance our budgets and have surpluses. In certain other years we shall just be able to balance our budgets, while in still other years we shall have to have deficits. I have announced the policy of the government to be to budget not for a surplus each year, as has been the ambition of ministers of finance in past years, but to budget rather for cycles and to face the certainty that if some adverse conditions strike the country it may be as a result of developments beyond our borders. It may be as a result of weather. There are several causes to which such conditions might be attributable, and it might be necessary for us to have deficits. It is impossible for me to place before the House of Commons now a five-year plan-that is a five-year budgeting plan. It is impossible because we have not completed our negotiations with the provinces, and we do not know within-well, I would take a figure of two hundred or three hundred million at any rate-what our expenditures will have to be as a result of agreements that we make with the provinces. That is a matter that we shall have to iron out.
This question was raised. I was appointed chairman of what was called a subconference of the dominion-provincial conference at the time it met in August, and the representatives of one of the provinces asked the same question. They said: "It is all right for you to ask us to enter into these agreements, but what are your plans? Can you tell us what your budget will look yke, what your statement of receipts and expenditures will look like in, say, the fiscal year 1948-49 or 1949-50?" I said in reply: "Yes. I can tell you that, on the assumption that our proposals are accepted; but I dare not tell you that without the deletion of a great deal of information, because it involves plans with regard to tax rates, corporation taxation, individual taxation and so forth, which simply cannot be made public." And I can no more make it public in this house than I could before the dominion^provincial conference. Therefore, a minister of finance, it seems to me. in this month of December in this year 1945, is limited to a statement of general principles. The general principles are that we shall have as our objective the balancing of budgets over a period but not to balance budgets every year. Some years we shall have surpluses, some years we shall strike an almost exact balance, and some years we shall have deficits.
That is a brief answer to the questions which the hon. gentleman has asked. It may be briefer than the exposition of the subject entered into by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. I do not know. But I have asked myself several times during the last year whether I should not make a speech somewhere in which I should tell the public of Canada how we hoped to finance and what methods we would use in financing for the next few years-to what extent we would raise money by borrowing, to what extent by taxation, to what extent if any by bank borrowings. But every time I approached the subject I backed away from it. I discussed it with the deputy minister of finance two or three times, and backed away from it because of the uncertainty inherent in that situation and necessarily arising from it. The uncertainty was so great. However, we did go as far as we could in the white paper on reconstruction last spring and also in speeches I made in the victory loan campaign, when I made similar statements. I cannot be more definite.
All we can do is to take it a year at a time. We have been definite about the present fiscal year: everything is before the house; and we shall have to be equally definite for the next year when we present our estimates for the next fiscal year and budget for that fiscal period.
I agree that we should' not go carelessly on hoping for the best, but should have some principles on which to proceed, and it may be possible to be much more definite if we are able to come to an agreement with the provinces. If we are not able to come to such an agreement-

Then there is a wide range in the amount which may or may not be payable to the provinces. As regards subsidy arrangements, we have not got down to that. I do not know what we shall agree to. I want an agreement with the provinces, but I cannot agree to an arrangement with them which will make our budgetary position impossible. I cannot do that. The old bad system would perhaps be better than that. The whole thing is that I cannot be definite about the future in the light of present uncertain circumstances.

I proceed with the suggestion that more can be given us than has been given, and that to withhold it is, first of all, to withhold from the people of Canada what is their own business, and, secondly, it is leaving it w'ith other people who are not as responsible as is the Minister of Finance.

It is of interest to all responsible people in business, because naturally they are full of anxiety and concern. Why would they not be? We are all full of anxiety and concern. We cannot see the future clearly. I do think, however, that we are entitled to ask the Minister of Finance to take the people of this country into his confidence. In saying this I repeat that there must be due regard to certain things concerning which he would be entitled to maintain certain reservations.

I think I ought to answer the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario first, as to' what extent the minister is really the watchdog of the treasury. He wanted information as to how far the Minister of Finance goes in checking expenditures. That is a long story. I have gone into it at various times in the past; I have been frank about it and my frankness has got me into trouble. I have been criticized in the newspapers for what I said, but I

think in the long run frankness is probably the best policy. I shall be frank again to-day. - The chief check that the Minister of Finance has on expenditures in time of peace, when we are proceeding on the basis of bringing in estimates in detail before parliament, is in the preparation of the estimates. Normally we begin about November of each year to ask the departments to submit their estimates for the coming fiscal year. The estimates come in; and the staff of the treasury board, without reference to the minister in the first place, go at those estimates and try to have them reduced. They are successful to a considerable extent in having t'hem reduced. But various departments demur, and some go even farther than that and vigorously and violently protest against the proposed cuts. The matter is then taken up by myself with the various ministers and by the treasury board with the various ministers, and after a considerable amount of argument the estimates are still further reduced until they reach the form in which they appear before the House of Commons.
When speaking in this house on a former occasion about non-war estimates I was severely criticized by one of the leading metropolitan newspapers for saying that I considered my responsibilities pretty well finished at that point; they criticized me for abdicating at that stage. But I really do not abdicate at that stage, because many of the expenditures to be made under items passed by the House of Commons must be made under orders in council passed pursuant to various acts of parliament. Time after time I have taken exception to those orders in council. They are then referred to the Department of Finance for study and report by the Minister of Finance.
So far as my own duties are concerned, I have often said that the most difficult thing is not the control of prices; the most difficult thing is not the borrowing of money; certainly the most difficult thing is not taxation; the most difficult thing is not housing; perhaps the most difficult thing, the thing that is hardest on the nerves is the perpetual watching of expenditures made under authority of orders in council. The reason it is such a strain is that unless the Minister of Finance is very careful, an order in council will be passed which in itself may be sensible and wise but which would set a precedent for expenditures to follow which would be most serious from the point of view of further financing or from the point of view of economy in expenditures. That is the practice in time of peace.

Supply-Finance
In. time of war the difficulties of being the watchdog of the treasury are greatly increased. They are greatly increased, not because expenditures have to be so much greater but because of the flexible system we have to have in time of war. We bring in a War Appropriation Act which enables money voted thereunder to be applied to almost any project or purpose. The various departments decide that money should be devoted to this, that or the other purpose, and the responsibilities of the Minister of Finance thereupon become much greater than if the scope of the expenditure were limited by a parliamentary item. That is the reason why all through the war the tendency of the treasury has been to force expenditures into the estimates as much as possible and out of the War Appropriation Act.
I am afraid I am making a self-righteous speech here, talking about other ministers and so on. The treasury may be wrong about this; in fact the treasury is apt to be very wrong in time of war, because action is more important in war than economy. Other ministers with the very best of intentions, men who get action and so on, desire flexibility. They desire the power to put money to this, that or the other purpose, and they find themselves up against this somewhat financially minded Department of Finance which is cramping their style all the time. I do not know whether on balance to take credit for these watchdog operations or not, but they go on to the best of our ability.
We have an institution called the treasury board. With the exception of the Minister of Public Works the other night, who, thank heaven, did say a good word for the treasury board, I cannot remember of anyone ever saying a good word on its behalf. We talk about putting a watch on expenditures, but how much assistance do we get in this house in watching expenditures? Nine-tenths of the speeches in this house are asking for bigger and better expenditures. That was the case all through the last parliament. While this session did not start out in that way, it finally got that way. If the government is making large expenditures, it is not because the ministers are trying to make those expenditures; it is because of public and parliamentary demands for those expenditures. That is why the expenditures are being made. At times I feel as though I am against the whole world when I try to keep a lot of these expenditures down. We just do the best we can, that is all, and keep them down.

I do not like to
repeat, but I think this will bear repeating. In 1938 we had 44.000 civil servants in this country, and we paid them $88,000,000. In 1945 we had 150,000 civil servants and the amount we paid them, for 1944-45 was $229,000,000, according to the return I got. That is about half our normal peace-time budget. My purpose in rising is first to bring that to the attention of the house and the country.
The other thing that I have in mind is this. We have 150,000 civil servants, and with three to a family, this means that 450,000 people in this country are living off 12,000,000. That does not take into consideration the number of civil servants working for the various provincial governments and for municipal governments. That is just a little more than Canada can stand. These 150,000 civil servants have been doing a job and a good job in this war. But that number must be cut down. They are not engaged in constructive effort; they are non-constructive, and what we want to do is put some of them back into useful enterprise.
I think that is one of the biggest jobs before the Minister of Finance, the treasury board and the government at the present time. I urge them with all the power at my command to try to cut down this overhead, so that we can cut down the cost of government in this country and reduce the burden of taxation on the individual taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Before the item carries, I
think I should answer the question asked me by. the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, who wanted me to give some indication of the activities of the wartime prices and trade board. It is hard to cover that subject in a few words. We have an annual report from the wartime prices and trade [joard which covers the work of the board fully. I presume -that the hon. member has lead that. He particularly referred to the question of subsidies. He intimated to me very kindly last night that be would be asking me something about subsidies, and I jotted down the main types of subsidies that are paid and the reasons why they are paid. When we imposed the over-all or general price ceiling in the fall of 1941 we realized that some provision would have to be made for imports. That is, if the price of goods went up abroad it would be impossible for importers to import those goods and sell them under the Canadian price ceiling unless they were subsidized. So the first important class subsidy which was authorized was the import subsidy, which has continued from that day to this. The tendency

Supply-Finance
through the years has been to take more and more articles off the subsidizable list. To begin with we subsidized any import, but with a little experience it became apparent that^ it was hard to justify the payment of subsidies on the importation of certain types of luxuries, so they were taken' off the subsidy list. Those are the import subsidies.
The second class of subsidies I want to mention is an interesting class. It was discovered that retailers were selling in some cases in the base period-the period was a few weeks in the fall of 1941-and that their prices during that period were based upon the purchase price of goods which they had bought perhaps six months before. In the meantime the wholesalers' price had gone up so that it would be impossible for the retailers to continue to sell, say in the spring of 1942 and later, unless they were able to buy the goods from the wholesalers at the prebasic period price, the price which they charged as early as the spring of 1941 or the fall of 1940. So we then paid these roll-back subsidies, subsidies which rolled the wholesalers' price back to the appropriate period which enabled retailers to sell under the price ceiling. That is a second class of subsidy.
As the years went by, costs increased1 in various ways to certain domestic producers; and while we have not recognized increased wages as a reason for the payment of subsidies, many other costs are recognized as a reason for the payment of subsidies, and domestic subsidies are paid to some industries to enable them to produce and sell under the price ceiling. That is the third class of subsidy.
Another class of subsidy, of which I believe there is only one example, is the milk subsidy, which was undertaken for the specific purpose, not of keeping the price at what it was during the basic period, but to reduce it two cents below what it was in the basic period, in order to prevent the cost of living index from rising unduly. That is a consumer milk subsidy, a very important subsidy, and virtually the only one of its kind. This is the fourth type.
The fifth which I should mention is the bulk trading losses. Some goods are purchased by government agencies and sold to the trade in Canada or to the Canadian public at a loss. This subsidy applies to dried fruits and to some other commodities which I have forgotten for the moment-it is immaterial.
But these are the main types of subsidies. These are the subsidies which are payable by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corpora. tion, which is the agency of the wartime prices and trade board.
In addition to these, there are production subsidies which are recommended and paid by the Department of Agriculture. They are for the purpose of encouraging or of maintaining production and to some extent correcting inequities as between farmers and other producers in the country. They are substantial. In that class would come the butter subsidy and the fluid milk subsidy-except this consumer milk subsidy I have mentioned; the canned milk subsidy, the cheese subsidies, and some others: there are certain other subsidies paid by the Department of Agriculture.
These are the subsidies. We are getting out of subsidies as fast as we can.

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER

It did so at the very time when it knew that meat production in Canada was going down by double the amount by which it proposed to increase the supply for overseas shipment. The minister will find, by analyzing his own statement at page 393, in the first eight months of this year 270,000,000 pounds less of meat was produced than in the same period last year, 30,000,000 pounds a month less, and the government, in the face of that, undertook to send 15,000,000 pounds more a month overseas. My question is: Why did you not bring in meat rationing then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The only point I wish to make is this, and it will all be found in the minister's own statement. He proposed in September to increase the amount of meat we were sending by 15,000,000 pounds a month, and to do that he asked the1 Canadian people to eat less. In the very same address and in his own figures he pointed out what the bureau of statistics had always known, that the production of meat in Canada as shown by the slaughterings of live stock was down by more than thirty million pounds a month. My question is: when the government knew that and knew it would have to bring in rationing, why did it not bring in rationing then instead of leaving it until September?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER

It was decided to bring it in long before September, but a great deal of preparation was necessary. I think it was decided about July. The middle of the summer, in the hot weather, is a bad time to bring in meat rationing, and there was continual argument about it. A great many people thought meat rationing would not
Supply-Finance

increase the amount of meat available for overseas; that there would be so much opposition to it, so much friction, and so on. We had a great deal of opposition and friction; we must not forget that. We had a strike of miners in Alberta lasting for more than a month following the introduction of meat rationing. We had a butchers' strike in Montreal, and we had endless delegations. We persisted, however, and it was the right thing to do; but the restoration- of meat rationing was not something to be entered into lightly.

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS REMAINING ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I suggest that the opposition to rationing, whatever it was, should not have been allowed to influence the government to postpone that decision when it knew it was increasing the amount of meat going overseas and when it also knew that at the same time production in Canada was down almost twice as much a month as in the previous year. The government under- * took to send an additional fifteen million pounds a month overseas at the very time it knew production was down thirty million pounds a month compared with the previous year. Yet it did not bring in rationing until September. The reduction in production was known to the government in January of this year. Its own statistics show that from 200,000 to 300,000 fewer hogs were killed each month from January onward during the first half of this year.

speechtext:
The question of income tax assessment of farmers and ranchers was raised some time ago in the house, and I undertook then to make a statement indicating the basis on which they are assessed, having in mind' two particular problems; first, cash versus inventory and, second, what might be called dispersal sales by ranchers and farmers of their cattle.
I am advised that farmers and ranchers are assessed on either the cash disbursed and cash income or on an accrual or inventory basis. The ca$h basis, as its name implies, takes into account only the cash received and the cash paid out during the taxation year. At the inception of the Income War Tax Act farmers as a class did not keep accurate accounting records, and to a lesser degree that still is substantially true. In the main they only keep memoranda regarding the money received and the money spent. Because of this, farmers, unlike other business concerns, were permitted to use the cash basis and to report as income that which they paid out, the difference representing the income on which they were taxed. This method fitted in with the factual position of farmers, and found general acceptance by farmers because it was simple and could be easily understood. As stated, they regarded that which they sold for cash in the year of sale and that which they bought for cash in the year of purchase as representing income and outgo. They set one off against the other, and the difference indicated their income for that year. This method of determining revenue and expense does not apply to capital assets that were bought or sold during the year, that is, farm machinery was

Supply-National Revenue
not an expense in the year of purchase. It was a capital expenditure and was subject to depreciation. Likewise machinery sold was not brought into revenue account.
The second system was, as stated, the accrual or inventory basis. This requires the maintenance of proper accounts and records, taking into consideration not only the cash receipts and the cash outlays but maintaining an accurate record as to inventory of live stock, grain and other revenue producing assets on hand at the beginning and end of each year, so that the cost thereof could be carried forward and offset against the sales in the year of sale. Likewise it required the maintenance of a record of accounts receivable and accounts payable. The number of farmers using this accrual basis is in fact very small. Generally speaking it is not their practice. They are not accustomed to it. They are not skilled in it and, generally speaking, they find it difficult and confusing. The practical application of the income tax law was therefore on a cash basis.
There were practically no objections raised to farmers reporting on a cash basis until the advent of war and the resultant increase in their sales, particularly of live stock at substantially increased prices. Herds had been built up by farmers. The cost of raising or purchasing, maintaining, attending and feeding the cattle had been allowed as an expense in years prior to their sale. Thus all expenses over successive years were taken during the successive years as an expense against whatever income there might be in those years from all sources. The herd, by natural increase or by purchase, continued to grow

that is, expenses continued successively over the years-but no substantial sale of cattle took place. Then a sale of a substantial portion of the stock did take place. The sale price as usual was income in the year of sale. The farmer perhaps felt aggrieved that in the year of the substantial sale of cattle he should be called upon to declare his income on the cash basis, even though that was the usual basis.
Now it is quite clear that he has laid the foundation over the years in respect of which his assessment should be levied, but the high rates of tax, together with the high income, with the resultant heavy, tax, creates in him a sense of dissatisfaction. His tax will be much higher than that which he has normally been paying over the past years. Not having felt the weight of sudh a heavy tax he feels that there is something wrong in asking him to pay a heavy tax in the year of substantial 47696-236
sale on the mere basis of relativity when compared with the prior years of small tax liability.
The taxation division, appreciating the difficulties and the concern of such farmers, under date of February 24, 1944, instructed the inspectors of income tax across Canada that any farmer or rancher who had previously filed his return on a cash basis but who desired to change to an accrual basis would be permitted to do so, and outlined the procedure to be followed in such cases. Briefly the procedure was as follows: First, ascertain, the inventory of cattle, grain, et cetera, on hand at December 31, 1935; second, tax that inventory as income of 1935 along with the income of 1935 previously reported; and third, adjust subsequent returns in accordance with the inventory at the end of each year.
The instructions also indicated that where actual inventories could not be accurately determined, a reasonable estimate of such inventories would be accepted, provided that in future the farmer or rancher took 'actual annual inventories. The inventory values were to be taken having regard to the appropriate stock market and grain market reports in the locality of the taxpayer at the various dates. The effect of this ruling was to spread the income arising from a substantial sale over a number of back years, including the year of sale, instead of considering the total receipts as income of the year of sale. This resulted in relief from an excessive tax burden to the farmer by ascribing his income to the years during which the inventory grew in value. .
This method is dependent entirely upon the farmer being prepared to go in future on an accrual basis and keep accurate records henceforth of cattle, grain, et cetera, inventories, accounts receivable, accounts payable, et cetera-in other words to maintain a proper accounting system, if he continues in business. There are no statistics of the number of farmers or ranchers who have changed from a cash basis to an accrual basis, although on general knowledge they are believed to be comparatively few.
Another problem arose in connection with farmers who were giving up business and selling their entire herd and inventories in a bulk sale. The claim was made that it was unfair to tax in one year the proceeds of the sale of stock which had been acquired over a number of years. Again it had to be pointed out that the cost of raising or purchasing that stock had been allowed as an expense of previous years, and having returned their income on a cash basis the cash received on.

Supply-Notional Revenue

a bulk sale was strictly income of the year of sale. It was realized, however, that some injustice would be occasioned by taxing on this basis, and the taxation division has permitted a spreading back of the proceeds of the bulk sale over a period of three to five years, including the year of sale.
In doing this several factors have to be taken into consideration, that is, the inventories, accounts receivable and payable, et cetera, at the end of each of the three or five years, and in many cases they have to be estimated. In any case relief from an excessive tax burden enures to the farmer. At page 2745 of Hansard of November 30, the hon. member for Souris suggests an example be given of how such a method would be worked out. We will take his arbitrary figure of a bulk sale in 1945 of $10,000. Assume that the farmer's inventory was as follows:
1941		   $1,000
1942		 5,500
1943		 7,000
1944		 8,500
1945		   10,000
Instead of taxing the total proceeds of the sale of $10,000 in 1945 the taxation division would be prepared, if there were no other factors to be taken into consideration, that is, accounts payable, et cetera, to deem $4,000 to be income of 1941 and $1,500 to be income of each of the four subsequent years. Most cases are not as simple as this, and all factors have to be taken into consideration in coming to a conclusion, but the fact remains in the case of a bulk sale where the farmer is going out of business, a reasonable adjustment is made. The inspector of income tax is always ready to discuss and recommend adjustments in the matter of bulk sales by farmers.
Questions have been raised as to the taxation of the proceeds of breeding animals. Inasmuch as^ the cost of purchasing or raising such animals has been allowed as an expense, the proceeds of sale represent taxable income. Indeed, the animal may be considered a breeder to-day and to-morrow be slated for re-sale. It is suggested that it is part of the farmer's merchandise; that is, what he deals in, and therefore on sale returnable as income.
With regard to the taxation of the proceeds of wheat participation certificates, the treatment of such is covered by order in council P.C. 6020 of August 1, 1944, which provides that any additional tax found due by reason of including the amount received from the encashment of wheat participation certificates with other income of the farmer in the year of encashment over and above that tax which would have been claimed if the farmer had 
been taxable in the year of receipt of the wheat participation certificate be remitted in any individual case.
Finally, it might be pointed out that by the 1944 statutes, section 4, subsection 5, chapter 43, provision is made for spreading a loss sustained by a farmer over a number of years, that is, one year back and three years forward; thus a loss sustained in 1944 could be claimed first against the 1943 income, and if not recouped in that year, then successively against 1945, 1946 and 1947.
I think that with that comprehensive statement on the record, hon. members interested who give it a little study will find that it covers in as clear a manner as it is possible to do it the whole question which the hon. gentleman has raised.

I am sorry that neither the Minister, of Trade and Commerce nor the Minister of Agriculture is here, for there is a question I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce under this item. It is brought to my attention that a large quantity of seed potatoes has been sold from the province of New Brunswick to Spain. All seed potatoes from the province of New Brunswick, I am informed, are sold or supposed to be sold through the special products board of the Department of Agriculture, except those that are sold to Venezuela and the United States and, I think, to Cuba. Under the regulations of the special products board the dealers or shippers of New Brunswick have the business divided between them on a quota basis. All exports are filled by the dealers and handled through the special products board. For1 example, F. W. Pirie Company, Ltd., of Grand Falls, N.B., got about 16 per cent of the' business; Porters Ltd., of Perth, N.B., got 16 per cent; McCain Products Co. Ltd., of East Florenceville, N.B., got 16 per cent; and Hatfield Industries Ltd., of Hart-land, N.B., got 16 per cent; the rest is divided among the smaller dealers. My information is that this large sale of seed potatoes to SpaiD
Supply-National Defence

is not being made through the special products board, as sales are supposed to be made; that the dealers or shippers of New Brunswick were not notified of the sale, that they were not given their fair share of the business, but that, in some way which should be explained, one dealer or perhaps more who possibly had some pull with the government was given the business. The special products board, I am informed, in reply to inquiries which were made a day or two ago, refused to give the quantities of potatoes that were being shipped or the names of the shippers. The board stated that it was done under a private agreement-whatever "a private agreement" may mean. The transaction, I believe, is contrary to the regulations; it is not playing fair with the shippers and dealers; it has the ear-marks of somebody having some particular pull; and it seems to me that light should be thrown on the transaction.
I ask the minister these questions: Have seed potatoes been sold to Spain? If so, how many were sold and at what price; what shipper or dealer supplied the potatoes, and if there was more than one, who were they and how much did each supply? What was the date of the contract and what were its .terms? Has an export permit been issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce; and if so, for what quantities was it issued, and when? Was the sale made through the special products board? If it was not made through that board, how was it made, and when? Why were not all the shippers or dealers in New Brunswick permitted to share in the business?
These are questions which, I think, should be answered. It is difficult to understand, if this sale has gone through, why it did not go through in the regular way and why all the shippers or dealers in New Brunswick did not get their fair share of the business.

I want to make a very short plea at this stage on behalf of the Canadian men and wromen in the army of occupation. I have had quite a number of letters, as no doubt all hon. members have, concerning conditions in Europe. I have summarized them briefly, and I should like to have the Minister of National Defence make some statement with respect to them. The most common allegation at the moment is with respect to the inadequacy and bad quality of food received by other ranks in the army of occupation. I was over there at a time when the black market situation was not too good, in France particularly, and United States and Canadian boys were penalized because advantage was taken of the quartermaster. It seems to me that if the men are suffering as a result of this, the Minister of National Defence may have means of investigating it.
The second important criticism which is commonly received is a protest about the lack of educational and vocational training for the occupation troops. I know that an elaborate scheme was set up to provide that material over there, and I wonder whether it has fallen down, whether the staffs have left the continent and the boys are limited to their own initiative.
The third matter is with respect to lack of proper recreational facilities. I have here a number of clippings from the Overseas Maple Leaf as late as the 28th and 29th of November complaining about that. I will not read them, but I should like to know what facilities are available. *
Of course there is also the perennial complaint, arising from considerable resentment, that former combat men, some of whom were wounded in action, are placed in the army of occupation while N.R.M.A. men have been returned to Canada. Might we have a brief statement from the minister explaining how he is safeguarding the morale of the army of occupation?

I wish to make a suggestion which I think is very timely. We have watched these estimates going through, having sat here nearly a month, meeting at eleven o'clock in the morning and sitting until eleven at night. Some of the estimates have been rushed through with the everlasting complaint of insufficient discussion. First of'all I would ask the government to set up
the rules of the house committee as one of the first of its acts at the next session of parliament, and to see to it that the committee meets. This session we had only one meeting, and only covered one-eleventh of the work of the previous committee. We brought in only one recommendation.
There is a second suggestion I have to make. The proceedings of the house in the last few weeks have become a travesty. We are ceasing to be an efficient instrument of democracy. We are losing our efficiency, and are ceasing to carry out the function of expressing the will of the people. This is a serious situation. I wish to make one complaint here and now, and to carry on from where the Minister of Labour left off the other day. I suggest that consideration be given the question of having estimates reviewed in a committee of the house before being brought on to the floor, and that when they are brought in here they come down as one item. All contentious debate could be held at this time. The external affairs committee passed through this house, to-day or yesterday, a resolution that the estimates of that department be put through the special committee first. There has been a resolution, and there is general agreement, that the national defence estimates should go to a committee on national defence and be discussed there. I shall not discuss the obvious advantages of being able to have experts questioned orally instead of having them here mumbling and passing over to the minister a piece of paper of which the minister may or may not have full comprehension.
I suggest further that we follow the British practice and institute a limitation upon debate. This session we have had long debates on the speech from the throne and on bill 15. They may have been important debates; possibly that on bill 15 was. But frankly we do a lot of beating the air. The debate on the speech from the throne was not of great importance. I suggest to the government that at the next session serious consideration be given to the limitation of these debates which have been so long, so that we shall not go through the travesty of bringing in estimates as we do and behaving as we have done in the last two or three weeks. Parliament is on trial at this moment as never before.

speechtext: I wish .to biing to the attention of the government a matter that I brought up before when the public works estimates were under consideration. On that occasion I spoke briefly, as I shall again, but I wish the committee to remember that the importance of my remarks is in inverse ratio to their brevity. I spoke then on the lamentable wages and salaries paid to those who work in this house to promote our comfort and convenience. I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Labour to the fact that there are several messengers on this staff, men who were in the army for four or five years and who served overseas who are going to be out of work when this house rises; and as far as I know no provision is being made by the government for their employment. That is a heartless and callous way to treat these men. The other matter is that the low salaries which are paid do not give the employees of this House of Commons a chance to live in decency, and I would strongly urge the government to review these wages and increase them, so that this parliament may give a lead to industry and commerce in the matter of wages and salaries paid to employees.
